web_title: 5. Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
book_title: Chapter 5: Management on Trial — Leading KPIs & Walking the Talk
title: Dials Before Profits
question: Are the operating indicators that lead profit moving the right way, what can a full 13,000-tonne platform earn, and has management's record earned the benefit of the doubt on getting there?

epigraph.quote: Our approach is built for the long-term, where returns build as utilization ramps up over time.
epigraph.author: Sidharth Birla, Chairman, Xpro India 29th AGM remarks, 20 Jul 2026 [88]

web_blocks.html: Reported profit is a lagging, noisy measure right now. Depreciation and interest on a new line arrive before its volume. Euro translation moves the bottom line, and there is only one reported segment. These indicators move first. "our calculation" marks figures derived from audited or company-published inputs.

web_blocks.takeaway: Volume indicators are improving. Price realisation and value mix, which carry the thesis, are still flat on audited data.

web_blocks.html: How we read the three that matter most. Utilisation is the first lever. Absolute tonnes are not disclosed, so the 35% quarterly output increase cannot be converted into a utilisation percentage. The second is realisation. Audited dielectric net sales per tonne produced fell 11% between FY23 and FY26 even while the narrative was about thinner, pricier film. Management concedes it chose "a slight softening of prices in anticipation of the creation of new capacities" [89]. The third, EBITDA per tonne, fell 46% from FY23 to FY26 and has begun to stabilise. The company publishes no segment margins, so these are the nearest observable stand-ins [39]. The 29.6% customer is, by arithmetic, mainly a refrigerator OEM. The reason is that ₹149.4 Cr exceeds all dielectric sales of ₹135.5 Cr [48].

web_blocks.title: Capacity and market runway: our arithmetic, not guidance

web_blocks.html: Management says India's base-film demand is about 15,000 t a year and that roughly 70% of it is imported [38]. Nameplate India capacity of 8,000 t is 53% of that figure. Including the UAE line, 13,000 t is 87% (our calculation). There are two cautions. The 15,000 t is an analyst-stated figure that management did not dispute. Installed Indian capacity is also not Xpro's alone. JPFL reports 10,000 t and SRF 4,500 t, which with Xpro's 8,000 t gives about 22,500 t against the same 15,000 t demand [7][68][59]. Globally, CEIA data quoted in JDL's IPO documents show 136,000 t of demand in 2024 rising to 195,000 t by 2029, so 13,000 t is 9.6% of 2024 tonnage and 6.7% of 2029 tonnage (our calculation) [43]. UAE tonnes must be sold abroad. Yet total company exports annualise to about ₹34 Cr. That is at most about 900 t if all were dielectric at ₹383/kg (our calculation).

web_blocks.caption: Illustrative earning power of the 13,000 t platform: OUR CALCULATION, not management guidance. Tonnes x ₹/kg ÷ 10,000 = ₹ Cr
web_blocks.takeaway: Below EBITDA we assume depreciation ₹42 Cr, interest ₹16 Cr, treasury income ₹9 Cr and tax 26%. The Low case roughly repeats FY26 profit. Only the High case needs both thin-film pricing and a 40% margin.

web_blocks.html: Inputs: realisation brackets the audited ₹383/kg (FY26) and ₹430/kg (FY23) and the verbal ₹480/kg modal price. Margins run from the 16-22% implied for FY26 to the lower half of management's 35-55% range [52]. Cross-check: management's "₹150 crores to ₹200 crores" per plant equals 90-100% utilisation of one 4,000 t line at ₹430-480/kg [39].

Capital intensity. The two new lines cost about ₹680 Cr for about 9,000 t, or ₹7.6 lakh per tonne. Barjora-2 at ₹212.3 Cr capitalised is ₹5.3 lakh/t. The UAE line is about ₹9.4 lakh/t, counting ₹358 Cr of CWIP plus ₹67 Cr of commitments and ₹44 Cr of leased land (our calculation) [8][36]. At ₹430/kg, revenue at full utilisation is only about 0.57x the capital employed. This echoes management's 2023 admission of a "relatively lower turnover to capex ratio" [37]. Barjora-2 covers its extra depreciation (about ₹8.8 Cr a year) and ECB interest (about ₹4.6 Cr) at about 26% utilisation at a 30% margin, or 39% at 20%. A 12% pre-tax EBITDA return on ₹680 Cr needs about 70% utilisation of the 9,000 t at a 30% margin. At a 40% margin it needs 53% (our calculation).

Who runs it. Sidharth Birla (68) is executive Chairman. He has been on the Board since inception and was reappointed from 1 March 2026. Managing Director C. Bhaskar (71) has 44 years with the businesses, and his term ends on 31 December 2026. Girish Behal (47) joined on 21 October 2024 as head of strategy and has been CEO since 27 August 2025. He is proposed as MD for three years from 1 January 2027. CFO V.K. Agarwal has been with the company since 2008 [8][88][94]. The Managing Director answers almost every question on the calls and the CFO speaks rarely, so the audit below quotes the Managing Director and unattributed management [95]. The vote on Mr Behal's appointment is not in the retrieved documents.

Governance. The Board has 10 directors, 5 of them independent. That is exactly the minimum for a promoter-side executive Chairman. Three independents left after ten years in July 2024 [8]. The auditor, Walker Chandiok, has given unmodified opinions. Its second five-year term ends at the 2027 AGM, and capex capitalisation is a key audit matter [8]. Promoters hold 40.31%, nil pledged. The fall from 45.26% to 40.32% is dilution, since absolute promoter shares rose by 1,05,750 [33][34]. Related-party flows are benign except one item. That item is the parent's ₹256.4 Cr guarantee of the UAE subsidiary's euro loan, 36% of standalone net worth (our calculation).

Pay versus profit. Seven key managerial personnel were paid ₹10.19 Cr in FY26, equal to 33% of standalone PAT (₹30.52 Cr) and 52% of consolidated PAT (₹19.6 Cr) (our calculation). Chairman and MD pay each rose about 12% in a year when standalone PAT fell 30%. Contracts allow commission of up to 2% of net profit each, within a 5% aggregate cap [8][96]. The CEO holds no shares.

Succession as risk and as opportunity. The risk is timing. Bhaskar (71) and technical head Bakshi (70) step back just as Barjora-2 ramps and the UAE line starts, and process know-how is the moat. The opportunity is continuity. Mr Behal has run operations since August 2025, so this is a hand-over rather than a surprise. Mr Bhaskar, who made most of the date commitments below, stays as mentor and chairs the UAE board [8][52]. The 70-80% fourth-quarter utilisation target was attributed to Mr Behal by Mr Bhaskar. It is therefore the first commitment of the new regime to be tested.

Calls on record are annual (June 2022 to May 2026) plus the 4 November 2026 half-year call. There is no revenue or segment-margin guidance. The yardstick is therefore what was said about timing, capacity, funding and mix [95].

web_blocks.takeaway: Three delivered, seven partial, five missed and two too early. Project dates are the weak link, and controllable balance-sheet promises the strong one.

web_blocks.html: Independent judgment. The record splits cleanly. Promises management controls directly were kept. These were early debt repayment, solar power, the dividend and no further parent equity. Promises that depend on European machinery, shipping and commissioning teams were missed four times in a row, by 6 to 21 months each. The Board's May 2026 claim that delays were "behind us" was overtaken within months. We would treat management's dates as the earliest plausible, not the central date. A one-to-two-quarter slip on UAE commercial operations would be unremarkable on this record. Disclosure habits matter as much as dates. Management withholds segment margins, tonnes by line and customer identity ("Customer accruals are never line-wise", 22 May 2026) [89]. Verbal numbers also do not always match filings. The ₹106.7 Cr borrowings figure excludes the subsidiary's loan. The verbal ₹470-550/kg modal price sits well above the ₹383/kg audited average. The global line-demand claim shrank from "almost 70 lines, 80 lines" by 2030 (2023) to "more than 20" (2026) without comment [37][88]. Against that, opinions are clean and no SEBI action is recorded. Contingent liabilities are about ₹5 Cr, and delays were acknowledged in releases (6 Nov 2025) [100]. The reporting can be relied on. The timetable cannot be taken at face value.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a confession about analysis. When a company is spending more on factories than it earns in a year, reported profit tells you very little about what comes next. You and I should watch the dials that move before profit does. For Xpro there are nine such dials, and I want to walk you through the ones that matter most, because they are where this story will either show up or fail to.

The first dial is how full the new Barjora line is. The company doubled its Indian capacity for capacitor film, the thin plastic that sits inside the components that smooth and store power in solar inverters, electric cars and ceiling fans, from 4,000 to 8,000 tonnes a year on 27 March 2026. Picture the stenter hall, the long oven that stretches the film, humming at one end and half asleep at the other. Management says the new line should reach 70 to 80 percent of its rated capacity in the January to March 2027 quarter. In tonnes that is 2,800 to 3,200, my calculation. What we actually know is thinner: output on the new line grew 35 percent quarter on quarter, the line lost about ₹7 crore in the first quarter of this fiscal year, improved by about ₹3 crore in the second, and was profitable at the EBITDA level in October [52]. EBITDA simply means operating profit before depreciation and interest. The company does not publish tonnes for the new line, so the 35 percent cannot be turned into a utilisation figure. That gap is the first thing I would ask about.

The second dial is the price per kilogram, and this one disappoints. From the audited tonnes and sales I get ₹430 a kilo in FY23 and ₹383 a kilo in FY26, an 11 percent fall, even though the story all along has been about thinner, dearer film. Management says it chose to soften prices ahead of new capacity, in its words "a slight softening of prices in anticipation of the creation of new capacities" (C. Bhaskar, 22 May 2026) [89]. Verbally the modal price today is ₹470 to ₹480, with 3.5 micron film above ₹600 and 3 micron near ₹900, but the audited average has not yet moved. The third dial is profit per tonne. Divide EBITDA by all the tonnes the group produces and you get ₹27,963 in FY23 falling to ₹15,127 in FY26, about 46 percent lower. The first half of this year, at ₹16,131, is a small step up from ₹14,707 a year earlier. So the floor seems to have been found, but a recovery has not yet been shown [36].

The other dials tell a milder story. The refrigerator-sheet business, which funds everything, grew volumes 26 percent in the September quarter against industry growth of 8 percent. Exports are 4.9 percent of revenue and up 82 percent in the half. Working capital has swollen: the cash conversion cycle, the days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers, went from 33 to 80 days. The new UAE plant has absorbed ₹360 crore of capital that earns nothing until it starts. And a single unnamed customer is 29.6 percent of revenue, which by simple arithmetic must be a refrigerator maker, since its purchases exceed all the capacitor film Xpro sells [8][48].

Now to the runway, and I want to be careful, because this is our arithmetic and not management's forecast. Management says India needs about 15,000 tonnes of this film a year and imports roughly 70 percent of it. With 8,000 tonnes in India and 13,000 once the UAE line starts, Xpro alone could in principle supply most of that demand, but it will not be alone: JPFL reports 10,000 tonnes and SRF 4,500, so India has about 22,500 tonnes of capacity chasing 15,000 tonnes of demand [7][68]. That is why the UAE line matters, and why exports must rise several times over. The bull would say global demand is growing about 7.5 percent a year, 13,000 tonnes is under 10 percent of the world's tonnage, and Xpro already sells where qualification takes months. The skeptic would reply that about 55,000 tonnes of new capacity is coming worldwide against about 59,000 tonnes of demand growth, so a pricing error has nowhere to hide [43].

So here is the earning power in three cases. In the Low case the new Indian line runs at half and the UAE at 30 percent, at today's ₹383 a kilo and a 20 percent margin: group EBITDA of about ₹76 crore and profit of about ₹20 crore, which is where FY26 was. In the Central case, 80 and 50 percent, ₹430 a kilo and a 30 percent margin, EBITDA is about ₹141 crore and profit about ₹68 crore. In the High case, 90 and 70 percent, ₹480 and a 40 percent margin, EBITDA is about ₹226 crore and profit about ₹131 crore. Notice how wide that is. The two new lines cost about ₹680 crore for about 9,000 tonnes, or ₹7.6 lakh a tonne, and at ₹430 a kilo even full utilisation produces only about 57 paise of revenue per rupee of capital. A 12 percent EBITDA return on that capital needs about 70 percent utilisation at a 30 percent margin. The reassuring part is that the new Indian line only needs to be about a quarter full to cover its own extra depreciation and interest.

Now to the people, because who runs the ramp matters as much as the machines. Sidharth Birla, 68, is executive Chairman. C. Bhaskar, 71, who has been with the businesses for 44 years and made most of the promises we are about to audit, retires as Managing Director on 31 December 2026 and becomes a mentor. Girish Behal, 47, who came from the polyester-film industry in October 2024, is proposed as Managing Director from 1 January 2027, subject to a shareholder vote whose result I could not find [88]. Is that a risk? Yes: the two most experienced operators step back exactly as the ramp starts, and know-how is the moat. Is it an opportunity? Also yes: Mr Behal has run operations since August 2025, so this is a handover and not a surprise, and the 70 to 80 percent utilisation target is the first commitment of his era to be tested.

On governance I find little to alarm me and a few things to notice. The Board has ten directors, five independent, which is exactly the minimum for a promoter-side executive Chairman. The auditor, Walker Chandiok, gives clean opinions and must rotate in 2027. Promoters hold 40.31 percent with nothing pledged, and the fall from 45 percent was dilution, not selling [33]. The cost of seven senior managers was ₹10.19 crore in FY26, a third of standalone profit, and the Chairman's and MD's pay each rose about 12 percent in a year when standalone profit fell 30 percent. The new CEO holds no shares. And the parent has guaranteed ₹256 crore of the UAE subsidiary's euro loan, 36 percent of its own net worth [8].

Now the part I enjoy most, the walk-the-talk audit. I took 17 statements from the six annual calls, the annual reports and the November 2026 call. In May 2023 Bhaskar said the first new line was "likely to start contributing in FY 2024-2025." It was declared commercial on 27 March 2026. In May 2024 he said "We should be operational definitely in the third quarter of the current fiscal," meaning October to December 2024, and in May 2025 he accepted that September 2025 was "a reasonable assumption" [38][39]. Three dates, three misses. The UAE line was guided for the second quarter of 2025 and is now at the dry-run stage. The tally: three promises delivered, seven partial, five missed and two too early to call.

What separates those columns? The kept promises were ones management controlled: repaying old bank debt early, turning on solar power ahead of schedule, not returning to the parent's shareholders for more equity, and holding the dividend. The missed ones depended on European machine builders, shipping and commissioning engineers. There is a second pattern: the company will not publish segment margins, tonnes by line or the name of its biggest customer, and some verbal numbers do not match the filings. The ₹106.7 crore of borrowings quoted on the November call leaves out the subsidiary's loan, so the consolidated figure is ₹273.7 crore [52][36]. And the global demand claim fell from "almost 70 lines, 80 lines" by 2030 in 2023 to "more than 20" in 2026, without explanation [37][88].

Why do the machines run late? Management's own explanations are mundane and, I think, believable: supplier-side problems, components damaged in transit that had to be replaced, and recurring external power cuts that slowed the Barjora ramp [97]. On the UAE line the main equipment is installed, but a second team of specialists has to inspect it before dry runs can start. As the Managing Director put it on 4 November 2026, "We are waiting for the Germans to come back, meaning it's a different team." He added that disrupted flights into Dubai were something the company "can't predict" [52]. That is honest. It is also the point: when delivery depends on a handful of European specialists flying into a region at war, the date is a hope, not a schedule. A careful investor builds slack into it, and management's record says the slack needed has been 6 to 21 months.

My independent judgment, then. The financial reporting is dependable: clean opinions, tiny contingent liabilities, no regulatory trouble. The calendar is not. I would treat any management date as the earliest plausible date and expect a quarter or two of slip, which is what the record would predict. This is a judgment about how much weight a timetable deserves, nothing more.

What would raise my confidence? The UAE dry runs starting between December and January. Commercial operations in the UAE by 31 March 2027. The new Indian line reporting tonnes, not only growth rates, for the fourth quarter. Turnover above ₹700 crore for FY27, which needs about ₹349 crore in the second half after ₹351 crore in the first. EBITDA per tonne above ₹16,131. As the Chairman put it at the July 2026 meeting, "Our approach is built for the long-term, where returns build as utilization ramps up over time." Utilisation is the word to hold on to.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A company can be careful with numbers and optimistic with calendars at the same time. Xpro's audited reporting is clean, its mechanical promises were kept and its project dates were not. The next two quarters supply the cleanest test the record has offered: dry runs, commercial start-up and the first disclosed utilisation of the new Indian line. Until then it is fair to treat the platform's earning power as a range from roughly last year's profit to several times it, depending on utilisation and film mix, not a point estimate.
